On section 1-Short title.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 1 carry?

Encouraged by the remarks of the Prime Minis-
Redistribution-

-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
ter a few days ago, in which he intimated first of all that he was not aware of the exact boundaries even of his own constituency in Alberta, and further encouraged by his subsequent remarks towards the close of his address on that occasion, -when he said, as reported at page 5347 of Hansard:
. 1 am not yet advised as to the whole issue m Alberta and not having had an opportunity to discuss it fully with anyone who could inform me, I am not going to do more than say that I believe the former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) with his conciliatory spirit, and the hon. member for VSee, R'ver (Mr. Kennedy) will have no difficulty m working out that problem.
And again, on the same page:
To-day the problem of the boundaries of Bow River is one of some difficulty, but I think there should be no really insurmountable obstacle in the way of its solution.
-encouraged, I say, by these remarks of the right hon. gentleman, I intend to devote a few minutes to the consideration of this question. What I propose to discuss is not so much the boundary of Bow River itself as the conditions in connection with the Calgary seats and the effect which that division has had on the rest of these constituencies. Before I come to that part of the discussion this morning, however, I must say that I share the views of many in this house, that redistribution left in the hands of those who are directly interested in its results is perhaps one of the unfortunate features of our so called democracy. After listening for several days, in patience and silence, to the somewhat bitter and acrimonious discussion -that has been carried on,
I do feel that the public interest would be better served if we could work out some practical method by which redistribution would not be left to us as members of the House of Commons. I do not however see the practical side of the proposal made by the leader of the opposition in that regard.
The leader of the opposition suggested that there should be set up a committee of supreme court judges, three from one side of the house and three from his party, I presume-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not say party; I said opposition.

There was
no other possible interpretation of the right hon. gentleman's words.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but I was very careful to make it clear that the government represents one side of the House of Commons while all those who sit opposite represent the Mr. E. J. Garland.!
other side. I did not try and was careful not to limit the opposition to one party.

But there still remains a practical difficulty, because this comer, or this group on this side of the house, has never yet been in the happy position of being able to appoint judges. Again let me point out to the right hon. gentleman that in the division he makes he implies, what I think he did right to imply, that judges, no matter how high spirited they may be, might under pressure of political influences revert to their former political partisanship.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Quite the
opposite was in my mind. I felt they would view matters judicially though with special knowledge.
Such a conclusion is inevitable from his suggestion that three be selected from one side and three from the other; he cannot get away from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You would have a political judiciary.

If on the
other hand we could secure something as intelligent, poor as it may be, as we have in our election act, it would not be so bad. The chief electoral officer is appointed for life, and if the chief distributing officer were appointed for life, not subject to the continual whims or influences of political parties, then perhaps we could get somewhere. Let me say this to the right hon. gentleman. I will support any practical proposal that will place redistribution beyond the power or influence of private members, but at the moment I see no practical way by which it can be done. If I thought it could be done I would support it heartily.
I come now to the second constructive proposal of the right hon. gentleman, namely, proportional representation. He says that if returned to power the party to which he belongs and has the honour to lead will once more bring up this question in the House of Commons-I presume with the intention of putting it through the house. I am very glad indeed to hear him say that, but my pleasure in the matter would be much greater if I did not have vividly in my mind a recollection of what has taken place in connection with this very question, during the government of the hon. gentleman. He was careful to say yesterday that his own ministry had introduced a bill into the house. He did not say just why it was not proceeded with but in soft tones he implied that it was because of the position of the Senate. What are the

Redistribution-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
facts? They are set forth in the journals of the House of Commons, sessional papers 1916 to 1930. In 1917 a motion was made by Mr. Turriff that necessary legislation should be enacted. There was a debate thereon which was adjourned as so often happens with these private members' resolutions. In 1921 a further resolution was introduced that some system of proportional representation should be adopted. An amendment was moved by Mr. Calder that a subcommittee should be appointed to consider the subject, and this was agreed to. The committee was appointed by leave, and there was a motion by Mr. Davidson to reduce the quorum, to report from time to time, to have leave to print and so on. The first report appears on page 391 of the records of that year. In 1922 there was a resolution to adopt the alternative vote method moved by Mr. Good, but the debate was adjourned. In 1923 there was a resolution to adopt the alternative vote method. That also was moved by Mr. Good who was a member of the group in this corner of the house. He came from Brant and I think he sat in the seat now occupied by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner). The motion moved in 1923 was agreed to. In a moment I will check it up and see what happened. It will be noticed that that was a motion to adopt the alternative vote method in constituencies like city constituencies. That was carried by the house at a time when my right hon. friend's party was in power. But no further move was made in that direction. In 1924 there was a resolution to adopt the alternative vote method, also moved by Mr. Good. The debate was interrupted by the six o'clock closing rule for Wednesdays.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I interrupt my hon.
friend? Has he the record there of what happened to the resolution regarding the alternative vote?

Yes, I
have the whole record. In the year 1924 the former Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) introduced Bill No. 128. The purpose of this bill as stated in the explanatory note was to make to the Dominion Elections Act the amendments necessary to provide for the single alternative vote at any election when three or more candidates had been nominated and only one member was to be returned. That bill was given first reading and then allowed to stay on the order paper. In 1925, the hon. gentleman introduced a similar
measure, the purpose of which was precisely that of the bill of the year before. All of us who sit in this comer of the house know perfectly well why that bill was introduced, why it was placed upon the order paper, and why it was given only first reading. The only reason was to prevent further embarrassing discussions of the subject from this comer of the house. It was nothing more or less than that. I have a too vivid recollection of what happened. Why was not the bill given second reading so that there could be an intelligent debate? Why was it not sent to a committee, if necessary? The right hon. gentleman would have had the support of this group, and it was no mean strength at that time. Why did he not challenge the Senate when with the two groups combined he had such an overwhelming majority as to make it beyond question that the bill would carry. But he went no further in the matter. According to the records of 1923, I find that Mr. Good, seconded by Mr. Brown, then in this comer of the house, moved a resolution This contained many whereases and ended up with the resolve that in the opinion of this house an alternative vote method should be adopted for use in future elections for this house in all single member constituencies where more than two candidates were running for election. After a debate thereon, the motion was agreed to without division. The records of 1923 show that. May I ask my right hon. friend why this legislation was not pressed through in view of the non-contentious character of the decision of the house on that occasion? In the same year another resolution was introduced by Mr. Good, again seconded by Mr. Brown. After many whereases it resolved that in the opinion of this house, for the purpose of demonstrating the working and effects of the system of true proportionate representation, one or more multi-member constituencies should be constituted by the redistribution legislation in which that system should be applied at the next general election. There was a chance to pass that resolution and pass that legislation. It was not a sweeping form of proportionate representation, such as is now proposed, but only a moderate experiment to see if it would work out and if it really was subject to all the frailities and flaws to which it is said to be subject. What happened? When the vote was taken, although the right hon. gentleman and the hon. member for Quebec East voted in fav-

our of the motion, among others, there was lined up the following Liberals against:
Mr. Benoit Mr. Binette Mr. Bouchard Mr. Boucher Hon. Mr. Cannon Mr. Dechene Mr. Deslisle Mr. Denis (St. Denis) Mr. Duff Mr. Fafard Sir Lomer Gouin Mr. Macdonald (Pictou)
Mr. King (Kootenay)
Mr. Maclean (Halifax), Mr. MacLean (Prince) Mr. Malcolm Mr. Marcil Mr. Martell Mr. Michaud Mr. Marler Mr. Mitchell Mr. Power Mr. Rinfret Mr. Roberge Mr. St-Pere Mr. Seguin.
There were five or six ministers who voted against that motion and I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman if he has consulted those ministers and received their consent as well as the consent of these various genial French Canadian members to the legislation which he now proposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I might say
that the matter has been discussed and agreed to in a Liberal caucus.

I am afraid that it was also agreed to by the party upon a former occasion. I am pointing this out in all kindliness because we do not want to be disappointed again. If the right hon. gentleman does come to power again we want to nail him down now to this principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
They are just kidding
the troops.

The hon.
gentleman's party has kidded us plenty.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have always voted
against it.

But on
other questions. I am not so sure that the promises of my hon. friend's party have been always implemented. I do not think they are in a position to cast any stones.
There is the record and the right hon. gentleman says that he will introduce a bill. I may say that if I am here at that time I will support it and I am quite sure that if the group in this corner is back again-I do not think there is any question but that it will be back in greater strength-it will give its full support to such a measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Do you think that promise is safe?

The right
hon. gentleman can rest assured that whatever government is in power, this group will support any measure for proportionate representation or even the single transferable vote.
[Mr. E. J. Garland.)
As a matter of fact if that is not done we will see that they get the opportunity.
There can be no two views as to the justice and the logic of the position taken in regard to the necessity for this alteration. I say frankly to any hon. gentleman present who is concerned with serving the public interest and getting just representation that there can be no two thoughts on this question. Let me give the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) another illustration. He heard the excellent one given yesterday by the leader of the opposition in connection with the actual results of the last elections. These results are wholly unjust and out of proportion to the actual votes cast.
I come now to the Irish Free State election of 1933. Ireland is a country in which proportional representation has been put into effect and in which it functions admirably. Indeed, so efficiently does it function now that the whole world was astonished at the rapidity with which the results were published after the general election of January, 1933. The complete fairness of this method was indicated in the figures that were published in pamphlet No. 73 of the Proportional Representation Society. The parties are grouped into two lots: the De Valera group and Labour who were cooperating and the opposition group consisting of the Cosgrave group, Centre and Independents. The De Valera and Labour group polled 770,968 votes and won 185 seats, or 9,070 votes per seat. The Cosgrave, Centre and Independent group polled 615,358 votes and won 68 seats, or 9,049 votes per seat, almost an identical number. Approximately 9,000 votes elected a member, exactly corresponding, as I have suggested, to the support that was given. It should be noted, however, as was pointed out by the Ottawa Citizen in an editorial the other day, that in these figures are included the university seats and the seat of the Speaker, the candidates for which were returned by acclamation. If we exclude these, we find that the total vote cast for the De Valera and Labour group was 768,889 and that 82 seats were won, or 9,376 votes per seat. In the other group, 613,666 votes won 64 seats, or 9,528 votes per seat, an almost exact reflection of public opinion.
_ Let us compare this with the British election in 1931. In Great Britain in that election the National party, formed as it is of many parts, polled 14,519,016 votes and won 491 seats, or 29,000 votes per seat. Labour on the other hand polled 6,649,630 votes, but won only 46 seats, this working out at 144,000 votes per seat, whereas the National party won its election and power on 29.000 votes per seat. No other argument is necessary than to give illustrations of that character. I admit

Redistribution-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
there are practical difficulties, geographical difficulties, difficulties of area and all that sort of thing, but none of them is insurmountable. In Ireland they have worked out this method for the whole nation on an intelligent basis under which, as I have just indicated, the results are as happy as they have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that this was tried for a number of years in British Columbia, in Vancouver, New Westminster and other places, and that after an earnest trial it was discarded?

It was also tried in Winnipeg. It operates as a single transferable vote method in Alberta for provincial elections with every satisfaction; so far as I know there is nobody in that province who is not satisfied with the results. Just because the forces of reaction were stronger in British Columbia than were the forces of progress is no reason for suggesting for a moment that the principle is unsound or impracticable.
I now revert to the question of the redistribution in Alberta and again I quote the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett):
To-day the problem of the boundaries of Bow River is one of some difficulty, but I think there should be no insurmountable obstacle in the way of its solution.
I am prepared to accept the words of the right hon. gentleman when he said that he was not even aware of the exact boundaries of his own constituency. I am prepared to accept his words when he said that he had not yet been fully informed as to the whole issue in Alberta. May I in a few words that will be as noncontentious as possible, indicate to him precisely, as I see it, the situation in my province?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have gone over the
map since.

I am very
glad. I had hoped that that had been done and that some reasonable arrangement could have been arrived at, but apparently it is hopeless. Calgary is a city of exactly 83,761 population. In the city of West Calgary my right hon. friend holds his seat. The city of East Calgary did the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Stanley) the honour to elect him. The city of Calgary with a population of 83,761 would, with the addition of a very small proportion of agricultural territory in its neighbourhood, perhaps with the addition of a very little beyond the surburban townships, have resulted in an excellent two-seat city, and on the principle that industrial population should be kept as closely as possible to itself, this would have been an excellent two-seat city. What has happened?
For some reason and I am not going to say for what purpose I think it may be-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There has never been
a two-seat constituency in the west.

I mean two constituencies to the city. I am glad the right hon. gentleman has helped me to clear that up. I do not understand why it has been divided virtually into three seats, for that is actually what has happened. It seems so illogical, so unfair to divide a city of that small size into three seats. On the same basis the city of Montreal would have about twenty-five seats, Vancouver between eight and nine, Winnipeg eight and Ottawa around five, with the addition of the country territory around; as has been done in the case of Calgary. Obviously this is unfair; it it not the just system of redistribution of which the right hon. gentleman has spoken.
The old East Calgary constituency embraced part of the city and a part of rural territory, about twenty-four miles wide by about thirty-six miles long running immediately north of the city. For some reason the hon. member for East Calgary desired to get rid of that and he abandoned his old rural East Calgary. He then also desired apparently to get rid of a part of industrial East Calgary, in fact a large portion, amounting, I am informed to 19,000 or 20,000 people out of a population of 83,000. For the new East Calgary is carved a channel down through the centre of the city and it is extended onward along the boundary of the Bow river down to a line south of Okotoks and then west to take in the Turner valley oilfields. This is an amazing constituency, an astonishing one to make. I would like to know why it was necessary to give up old rural East Calgary or industrial East Calgary. Surely these people were faithful to the hon. gentleman in the last election, but now he is willing to cast them to the chilly waters of Bow river and to betake himself to the warmer and ever green pastures of Turner valley. I cannot for the life of me understand why the hon. gentleman did this unless he is afraid he cannot be elected again in the old constituency of East Calgary. That may not be just to him; I do not know. But that is the only reason that comes to my mind as possible at the moment for his extraordinary action.
Now will hon. gentlemen note that having once made such a distribution of the Calgary population and having taken in a large portion of the old constituency of Macleod, the constituency of Macleod was left without sufficient population, and so Macleod is ex-
5478	COMMONS
Redistribution-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
tended out into the southern portion of Bow River. That is the first dislocation .that results from what the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) has decided upon. Medicine Hat, a constituency that like the southern Saskatchewan seats suffered from drouth for many years, and depopulation consequent thereon, had fallen below the necessary quota. Its actual population was 32,709, and evidently it was desirable to build that up. Now the constituency of Lethbridge had a population of 47,871, or over 3,000 more than was required for the quota even if 44,000 was to be regarded as a fair quota for rural constituencies of the character of Medicine Hat, Macleod and so on, which by the way I would not for a moment attempt to sustain. It is my impression, and I am upheld I think by all fair-minded persons, that city constituencies should always have a larger unit of representation than rural areas which are more difficult to cover, and for various other reasons which were given in the discussion yesterday.
Be that as it may, here was a constituency absolutely adjacent to Medicine Hat from which a surplus population could be drawn without injury either to the people themselves or to the sitting member. It would not have disposed of his seat or affected him in any way whatever. It would have taken in a few townships from the eastern side of Lethbridge and added them to Medicine Hat, and in that way built up its quota to a fair degree anyway. But instead of that the new Lethbridge constituency is left with a population of 46,401. Again I ask the question, why? It has been said, because the people living in the eastern townships of Lethbridge had a greater community of interest with Lethbridge than with Medicine Hat. That argument, if it is valid in that case, must be valid in other cases, some of which I shall cite in a moment or two. But it is not valid. It has never been regarded as valid. Look at the shifting around of population all over this country in this present redistribution. The convenience of the people concerned in a district must sometimes be affected by the actual requirements as a result of over- or under-population.
Medicine Hat, then, had to have population, and so they came to Bow River and took a second bite at the cherry, and they have just about destroyed it at that. The second bite runs tip along the Canadian Pacific railway line to just west of the town of Strathmore. The right hon. leader of the government knows as well as I do that the interests of the people of Strathmore and of Gleichen and of those 
little towns in between are far closer to those of Calgary from which Strathmore is distant twenty-eight or twenty-nine miles, and from which Gleichen is distant forty-eight miles, than they are to those of the city of Medicine Hat, from which they are distant some 132 miles. But for some purpose, population or other, the boundaries are moved up to embrace the towns of Strathmore and Gleichen.
It just happens by a strange turn of the wheel of fortune that I reside in the town of Gleichen, and therefore under this redistribution I will reside in the constituency of Medicine Hat. But, Mr. Chairman, I am not protesting on that basis, and for this reason: When I was elected in 1921 the constituency of Bow River ran far north of Drumheller and embraced my farming place and my home town. After the hon. gentlemen to my right, the Liberal party, redistributed the constituencies in 1924 that constituency was shortened up considerably, by 27 or more miles, and it left me just 27 miles outside the boimdary of my own riding. So this is the second time that I have been redistributed out of my constituency. But notice that whilst since 1921 I have resided 27 miles outside of my constituency my good friends in the constituency have been loyal to me and have elected me three times, in 1925, 1926 and in 1930. So I cannot argue that being resident outside the constituency is any great handicap in my case, nor would I so argue. As a matter of fact, I have sufficient confidence in the loyalty and intelligence of the people of that portion of Alberta and of western Canada to know that it does not much matter what is done in regard to that particular seat. The only thing I am pointing out to the right hon. gentleman is that this injustice is being done to the population in Strathmore and Gleichen. It is utterly unjust to Strathmore especially, and to a slightly lesser degree to Gleichen, to be tacked on to the city of Medicine Hat in the Medicine Hat constituency 132 miles away, while they are respectively only 28 and 48 miles away from the city of Calgary.
There may be an explanation for all these things but I cannot for the life of me see what it is. When I learned what was being done I did what was expected of me in the ambit of my duty. I saw our representative on the committee, the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), discussed the matter with him and told him that I looked upon this as a quite unfair form of redistribution, and he unavailingly took the matter up with the chairman of the subcommittee, and came

Redistribution-Mr. Stanley
back to me and said, "You had better prepare an alternative map." I went to work and prepared an alternative map, no easy task for one without an adding machine, but we prepared one and I submitted it to the whole caucus of our group on two occasions, and on two occasions they endorsed it as the fairest in every way. It displaces no person from his riding. It displaces materially no boundary line, except for a township or two, shifting them around a little, and it gives a fair unit of representation. Let me point out what it is. Under the proposal that I made both to the subcommittee and to the main committee, Macleod would have 41,855; Lethbridge,	41,011;	Bow River, 41,565;
Medicine Hat, 40,347; and the two Calgary seats 47,600 or 47,700 apiece, as best determined between the two sitting members for Calgary. It would have left Calgary still a two-constituency city. That is the feature evidently that it was thought desirable not to retain. The map I have submitted is absolutely fair. It disturbs nobody, and it leaves the boundary lines just in the general direction they were in before.
When this matter was discussed it was pointed out that that "impassable river" called the Bow river should be regarded as the boundary line and should be a factor in the redistribution. But, Mr. Chairman, strangely enough the impassable character of rivers has not always been used as a reason for a just redistribution but frequently has been used for an unjust redistribution, as in this particular case. The Vegreville constituency was extended north over an impassable river over which there is only a single bridge in the whole district, and it was extended to embrace a Ukrainian settlement. I have no objection whatever to that. I think that was the intelligent thing to do and I am raising no objection, but I am pointing out that a river was crossed although it was an impassable river. Let us take a look at the Bow river. In this very portion of the river that is under consideration there are no less than three splendid provincial bridges, steel structures, and traffic moves freely to and fro, winter and summer. It is the height of absurdity for any hon. gentleman to contend that the river is any longer an impassable boundary. The community of interest between one side and the other is complete. As a matter of fact, as the right hon. leader of the government knows, the population of that district south of the river, the Arrowwood district, travel across the river either at Cluny, at Gleichen or at Carseland and move on up to Calgary when they take their motor trips to the Calgary
stampede or for business reasons or to purchase supplies. The right hon. gentleman knows that as well as the hon. member for East Calgary. Yet this form of redistribution is to be enacted. Let me assure the house and government, and particularly the government, that in my view they would be well advised to reconsider the distribution of these six constituencies; only six are involved. The boundary lines of North Calgary on the north side, Bow river on the north side and Medicine Hat on the north side remain practically unaffected, except for a small jog to take in East Coulie. To that, again, I have no objection But it does not affect any of the constituencies in. the north of the province. Apparently it does not concern them. Those six constituencies might be redistributed on a fair basis; in my view the present basis is quite unfair. It disturbs the lines everywhere, disturbs the population everywhere. The point I wish to make this morning is that Calgary should not be divided into three seats, because such a change would be an injustice to the labour element of the city. It would weaken their position. Secondly Gleichen and Strathmore should not be tacked on to the Medicine Hat riding.

I shall not deal with the first part of the address of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in connection with the general subject of the electoral system. At this time it is an academic question, because we have long since passed the point where we must make any decision on matters of that kind. An interesting point, however, and an interesting piece of information which I think should be extended to the house and which the hon. member avoided very carefully was an analysis of the condition of representation in the legislature of the province of Alberta. As he intimated we have proportional representation in force in two of the cities, and the alternative vote in the provincial constituencies throughout the province. Therefore we should have a fair report from the results of the elections in those places. I regret I am not able to give the exact figures, but I understand there are in the neighbourhood of sixteen members, all told, who are not listed as supporters of the government, and whose aggregate vote exceeds that of all the government members put together. There is a chamber of sixty-one members. The government party in that legislature has a very large majority, but the party in majority holds office on a minority vote-a very considerable minority vote. Some time later we may be able to discuss that situation.
Redistribution-Mr. Stanley

However, coming to the immediate question which concerns us to-day in regard to redistribution in the province of Alberta and particularly that part of it which refers to the constituency of Bow River, first allow me to deal with the map which the hon. member himself prepared. This matter was fully discussed in committee; all representations were made there. The subcommittee met dozens of times and discussed the whole situation. In my view the rehashing of these details before the house serves no useful purpose. May I emphasize the fact that the hon. member who has just spoken stands out as the lone objector from the province of Alberta. There was agreement between the two hon. members representing the Liberal and Conservative parties. There may have been some small objections, but there have been no serious objections raised by representatives from other constituencies in the province. Some other hon. members may have some objections concerning the particular constituencies to which the hon. member has referred, but we have not heard of any serious objection being taken. In a few moments I shall deal with the details of his remarks.
First allow me to take the map which he has presented. It is a model of straight lines; there is no question about that. It is made with the idea of having straight lines, without any consideration for natural boundaries. The hon. member has been the author of these proposed straight line constituencies, and he still insists upon placing those straight lines to suit his own convenience. In our redistribution we took cognizance first of natural boundaries and secondly of community interests. In spite of what the hon. member has said, that section of the province of Alberta located south of the Bow river never has had and has not at the present time any community interest with that portion north of the Bow river, and particularly those people living in the Drumheller valley. To most hon. members these names may be only terms, but to the people living in the province of Alberta they mean more than that.
The constituency of Bow River came into existence in 1924. I am informed it was formed from the leftovers, after all the rest of the province had been redistributed. I have no doubt about that. Certainly it presents a leftover constituency, and as Bow River exists to-day I consider it has the most unfair representation of any'portion of the province of Alberta. The hon. member proposes straight lines to continue the condition existing in Bow River to-day. To that 
the committee cannot agree. Personally I certainly cannot agree to it. I state that the constituency as framed violates every idea of fair representation. Let us turn to the constituency of Macleod, to which the hon. member has referred. That portion of the constituency of Bow River south of the river which now becomes part of the constituency of Macleod naturally belongs to Macleod. It has and always has had a community interest with Macleod that no other constituency can claim. It extends eastward to the Bow river, and in spite of what the hon. member has said, there is an insuperable barrier between the Macleod constituency on the west and the Medicine Hat constituency, as proposed, on the east. It is a natural boundary. Having lived in that portion of the country, having covered almost every yard of that whole country from top to bottom by horse and otherwise, I know the country; and I know this, that the farmers of the early days who came and settled west of the Bow river came over to the Calgary and Edmonton railway and marketed all their grain in the Calgary and Edmonton towns prior to the construction of the present railways. That country now is traversed by two other lines of railway running generally north and south, and it is covered by some of the most excellent highways of any province in the country. So there is a community of interest beyond dispute.
Now the hon. gentleman says that Macleod is over the quota. It is, I admit. Personally it was my desire that a portion of Macleod should still belong to the proposed East Calgary constituency. But it was represented that it would be preferable from the standpoint of the member representing Macleod that that portion which would naturally come in should remain in Macleod. Personally I have no objection whatever to it coming in. It shall not go through without my first registering a criticism and protest against it, no matter whether it has been agreed upon or not.
My criticism applies to western Ontario. The proposal is to go into three historic counties of Ontario, namely, Bruce, Perth and Oxford, and to eliminate one seat from each of those counties. I do not know that I have any objection to the union of counties, where population and areas warrant only one representative. That procedure may be proper, if it were done fairly and with a spirit of justice. I wish to speak concerning that part of the county of Perth which I have the honour of representing, namely South Perth. The proposal is to unit the two constituencies in the county of Perth into one seat. But that is not the proposition which will come before this House of Commons. The proposal which will come before us is to unite North Perth and South Perth, with the exception of two townships. It is suggested that if these historic townships are left in the constituency the population of Perth will be too high. That is the excuse given.
rMr. Casgrain.]
Let me point out what the provincial government has done in their redistribution of the county of Perth. Apparently they thought Perth had not sufficient population. They united South Perth and everything in South Perth with everything in North Perth, and by some process of elimination or of moving through the air or under the ground they have added the town of Palmerston in South Wellington to the county of Perth, increasing the population one way and proposing to decrease it in another. There is only one reason for taking the townships of Hibbert and Fullanton out of South Perth and putting them into South Huron. It was done for political purposes, to weaken the Liberal candidate who will run for the county of Perth in the next federal election. There was only one reason why the provincial government took from another county the town of Palmerston and added it to the county of Perth; it was done to load the dice, to stack the cards.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to refer briefly to the political history of the county of Perth, showing that from 1867 right down to the present day North Perth-not altogether consistently, but almost consistently-has elected a Conservative to the House of Commons; and you will find that South Perth has done exactly the opposite, that since 1867 South Perth has voted Liberal with the exceptions of 1911 and 1917, 1911 being the famous reciprocity election, and 1917 the war time election. My point is that in uniting South Perth with North Perth the government should have been fair enough to take the chance on the record of the elections even going back to 1867. It is a horse race, it is practically a tie, a neck and neck race, in South Perth and in North Perth. But they are not fair enough to take all that comprises South Perth; they take out two townships with a population of over 3,000 and add them to South Huron. Now what is the reason for that; what is the explanation? Is it not to handicap the Liberal candidate when he runs in the whole county of Perth and give an advantage to the Conservative candidate? TLat is not fair. It cannot be defended in any way, mathematically or geographically. I would like hon. members to look at the map of the county of Perth. It will be seen that what they propose to do is deliberately to reach over the fence and take two historic townships which have been in South Perth since confederation, for purely political purposes to take them out of Perth county and put them in another county. I want to be perfectly fair and candid about this matter; there is not a Liberal in South Perth who would be opposed to the joining of the whole of South Perth with the whole of North Perth, making one seat for the county and taking their chance, win or lose. But in this way the government and the committee are taking an unjust advantage, doing an injustice to the Liberal party and the Liberal candidate, whoever he may be. There is no justification for it in respect of population, as I propose to show.

speechtext: The house again in committee on Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons-Right Hon. R. B. Bennett- Mr. Stirling in the chair.

When the committee rose at one o'clock I was putting some figures on the record in regard to the population of Perth county. Under the last census the population of the entire county of Perth is about 51,000, and the proposal is to take out the townships of Hibbert and Fullarton from South Perth and add them to South Huron, which would bring the population down to about 47,816. The population of Oxford, if it goes into one seat, will be 47,825. The Prime Minister, in correcting me this morning with reference to what had been said in regard to the claim that Montreal might ask for 24 seats, said that the unit of population was not always a factor in redistribution. With that I agree.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was hardly put that
way-not always the only factor.

I accept the correction. I am going to attempt to show what the position is with regard to the population of some of the other constituencies that are left untouched by this redistribution, and I am speaking only of the province of Ontario. It is proposed now to take the town of Clinton and the township of Goderich from South Huron and put them into North Huron. I mention it now only to show how the figures will work out. If that is done it will make the population 26,095 in what will be the riding of North Huron after the redistribution. In regard to the proposal to take the two townships of Hibbert and Fullarton from South Perth and put them into South Huron, with the town of Clinton and the township of Goderich taken from South Huron and put into North Huron, and two townships from South Perth put into South Huron, it will have the effect of giving South Huron a population of 19,085. That appears to be a low figure, and it is. I would point out however that in the province of Ontario there 	,
are some constituencies that are lower than that and they are not being touched by this redistribution. For instance, there is the constituency of Glengarry, with a population of 18,666; there is Haldimand, 21,428; and there is Brant, 21,202. These are all represented in this house at the present time by supporters of the government. And when we come to analyze some of the counties where there is only one member we find that the population far exceeds the population that Perth will have under this plan of redistribution. Perth, with the two townships out, the townships to which I have referred, would be 47,816. We have Lincoln, represented by one member, with a population of d4,199; there is Welland, represented by one member, with a population of 82,731; and there is Nipissing, also represented by one member, with a population of 70,204.
I quite agree with the Prime Minister ;herefore that the unit of population is not always the only factor in redistribution. I hope I have the right hon. gentleman correct this time. There are many constituencies far below the unit and many far above, and I know it is quite difficult to deal with this redistribution and balance the units of population.
I come back now to my own county of South Perth. In regard to the joining of the two Perths, I say again, as I said before the adjournment at one o'clock, that I have absolutely no fault to find with this proposal. As a matter of fact, I am and always have been in favour of it. The constituency of South Perth is low in population, less than 18,000. Yet under this bill it is proposed to take away almost 3,500 of population. I have always been under the impression that there was only one fair way in which to effect a redistribution in my riding. That was 'by joining the whole of the Perths together. There is no reason for taking two townships out of South Perth. It is an injustice to the people who live in those townships.
Let me enlarge on that for a moment. This morning the hon. member for Calgary (Mr.. Stanley) spoke about the community spirit. I quite agree with what he said. These two townships have been in South Perth ever since confederation and it is now proposed to move them to South Huron. I know that in some cases these matters cannot be adjusted but the only equitable and fair way to make an adjustment here is to leave these two townships where they have been since 1867. I know that it will probably be said that on the basis of the 1926 and 1930 elections there was not very much difference between the Liberal vote in South Perth and the Conservative vote in

Redistribution-Mr. Sanderson
North Perth. The figures for the 1930 election show that in North Perth the Conservative candidate was elected by a majority of 863 while in South Perth I had a majority of 717. Without taking out these two townships, the Conservative candidate would have an advantage of 146. This goes to prove the statement which I made this morning that since confederation the elections in the two Perths have been more or less of a horse race. But under this bill they do not propose to leave it that way, they propose to take out the townships of Hibbert and Fullarton. In the 1930 election the township of Hibbert gave me a majority of 245 and the township of Fullarton, a majority of 45. This makes a total of 290, which added to 146 will give the Conservative candidate in the next election an advantage of 436. Some hon. members opposite may say that that does not amount to very much. But why disturb South Perth at all? Why not leave it as it is so that there will be an even break between the south and the north, so that the next candidate may have a fair show and a fair run?
I have no desire to delay this committee nor do I want to break any agreement which may have been made. I am perfectly willing at all times to take a sporting chance, but there has been no justification for disturbing townships in South Perth. I have always been under the impression that county boundaries should be adhered to as far as possible in making a redistribution. If that principle were followed we would have a different picture to-day in western Ontario. Bruce county would be one seat and the same with Huron, Oxford, Middlesex and perhaps many other counties in the province. I am of the opinion that one hon. member is quite sufficient to represent a whole county in the House of Commons. I am sorry the Prime Minister has vacated his seat as I had a plea to make. I do not want to be misunderstood in making this protest. There has been an agreement arrived at and it may be said that I was a party to that agreement. But it cannot be an agreement when one has given his consent under pressure. If the agreement is not fair there is no reason why this committee could not adjust it and make it fair. I am asking for no special privileges, I ask simply for fair play. It will not be fair unless the whole county goes into one seat. If the committee in its judgment decides that there shall be no change, let it go at that but I am inclined to think that the good farmers of South Perth and North Perth will resent the fact that the whole county has not been joined together and that townships have been taken away. I think they will come to the same conclusion
as I have, that an unfair advantage is being given to my opponent.
If the county of Perth were made into one riding it would make one of the largest rural ridings in the province of Ontario. It would be, a rural riding inferior to none in the whole province. There would also be large manufacturing interests in the riding. The city of Stratford is a divisional point of the Canadian National Railways and there are about seven or eight hundred railway employees. The railway vote in Stratford has always been the deciding vote in an election. There will be the towns of St. Mary's, Mitchell and Tavistock, as well as six or seven smaller villages.
I ask only for fair play in this matter; I ask that these two townships which have been in the riding since 1867 be not interfered with. If that were conceded there could be no criticism. There cannot be any criticism where justice is rendered, but there can be and will be severe criticism if injustice is done and the whole of South Perth is not included in this amalgamation with North Perth.
I want to say this about my good friend the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MaoNicol): I have no fault to find with him. He has had a very difficult task to perform in this redistribution in Ontario. He has had many problems that must have been on his mind day and night. He has always been very courteous and fair with me any time we have had any conversation and I appeal to him as one coming from the city of Toronto and as one who, once he gets his nomination, is, as I said this morning, elected. He does not know what an election contest is; he has no handicaps; it is only a question of a majority or of thousands of a majority in the city of Toronto. I ask him to put himself in my position to-day. Will he be a party to handicapping me or any other gentleman who happens to be the Liberal candidate in Perth? Be fair about this. Never mind about these agreements if they are unjust. Now is the time to remedy that; now is the time for this committee to put itself on record and I appeal especially to hon. gentlemen opposite to be fair in regard to joining the two Perths. I say again that I am not pleading for any advantage; I am pleading only for justice, fair play, an even break and a chance for the Liberal party in the next general election in the county of Perth.

I want to thank the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), who has just taken his seat, for the very kind Remarks which he has made in reference to the committee and myself. I can also say that all my negotiations and those of the

Redistribution-Mr. MacNicol
committee-and I think I can speak for all the committee in this regard-with all the Ontario members have at all times been on the same plane on which the hon. member was so kind as to say I had negotiated with him on behalf of the other members of the committee.
I suppose I ought to be very careful in what I am now going to say because I may be treading on dangerous ground. Private members cannot make any prophecies or references as to what may be done in the future. The situation referred to by the hon. gentleman was, as he knows, not in our original picture. I am not going to refer to any reasons for changing the original picture; 1 suppose throughout the country many original pictures were changed, but in the final picture a situation resulted that I must confess we tried to avoid from the beginning. I believe all the members of the Ontario committee set out with the object of affording each hon. member an opportunity to return to his riding in so far as the redistribution was concerned. I am happy to say that with the exception of only the hon. member representing South Perth and the hon. member representing North Perth (Mr. Wright), every member from Ontario will have a free contest, one might call it, for election without being in opposition to anyone now in the house. The situation is that in the picture which finally resulted, in one lone riding my two good friends the hon. member for South Perth and the hon. member for North Perth may be nominated in opposition to each other in the next contest. The hon. member for North Perth does not desire this situation any more than does the hon. member for South Perth. We did not have to change the riding of the hon. member for North Perth so far as population went because he had approximately 34,000 and at the commencement we did not propose to alter it. Naturally he has a very strong case on which to oppose this bill, but I hope he does not do so; I hope he will accept it just as it is. In the next contest he appears destined to be up against one of the ablest members opposite, certainly one of the best speakers in the country, a thoroughly experienced organizer and a man with a great prestige in the western part of Ontario. I am sympathetic towards my warm friend the hon. member for North Perth because he will have a contest on his hands.
Give him a divine mandate.

What I started out to
say a moment or two ago was this: After 
the next general election, if all the prophecies my hon. friend, the member for South Perth, has been making about the result of the next election come true, if he is elected he will then >be sitting behind the then prime minister. If he is not elected and his prophecy in regard to the success of his party comes true, he will be the defeated candidate in that riding. If I am not treading on ground I should- not tread upon, perhaps the then prime minister will appoint him to a safe seat in the Senate if he will accept it.

Will my hon. friend
permit me? I made no prophecies about the coming election except in regard to Toronto and I said that I thought in that city, after the next election, perhaps three or four Liberals would be returned to this house. I never make prophecies.

Not in the speech the
hon. member has just made, I quite agree with that, but in many prophecies in former speeches. I want to speak in the same courteous manner as my hon. friend did, because I do not want to raise animosities as they get us nowhere. With the other members of the committee I want to see the whole Ontario schedule go through, but I should like to refer to a few figures in connection with those presented by my hon. friend. The present picture so far as the three ridings that are proposed for the counties of Perth and Huron are concerned, will be as follows: Constituency-	Population

We had to have some ratio of population to go by as a basis for these ridings and on examining the tables we found that in the proposed riding of Perth there is contained in the city of Stratford, the town of Listowel, the town of St. Mary's and the town of Mitchell-I am not sure whether it is a town, but I will give it that distinction anyway-a total of 25,808, or an urban population of over one-half of the new riding with a popu-iation of 47,816.
In connection with North Huron with a population of 26,095, there is an urban population of 6,239 and in Huron-Perth, with a population of 22,656, there is an urban population of 3,352. That strikes me as pretty fair ratios of population for those three ridings. One of them, that is Huron-Perth, is almost entirely rural. The riding of North Huron is not as largely rural as Huron-Perth, having twice the latter's urban population, and therefore it should have a larger unit than Huron-Perth. The riding of Perth itself, be-

Redistribution-Mr. MacNicol
ing over fifty per cent urban, should have a larger population than either of the other two. The fact that the city of Stratford has a population of 17,742, in the riding of Perth entitles that riding to a considerable larger unit of population for representation in this house.
As far as the townships are concerned the riding of Perth will have eight townships and four urban municipalities; North Huron nine townships and three urban municipalities; Huron-Perth eight townships and one small urban municipality; it therefore is much more rural than either of the other two.
The hon. member for South Perth has referred to Toronto. I shall give a few figures with regard to the city of Toronto, not with a view to criticizing what has been said at all, but simply to show that the city of Toronto has a very substantial unit for each of its members. Under the last redistribution there were twelve members for the county of York and the city of Toronto, which together may be called urban, the unit being 53,970. As a result of the present redistribution each of the 15 members proposed for the county of York including the city of Toronto will have a unit of 57,537, or approximately 4,000 more than after the last redistribution.
Taking it in another way, at the census of 1921 the two counties of Huron and Perth had a population of 97,731, and returned four members, so that the average unit was 24,443 as compared with the unit for the entire province of 35,776, which gives a percentage of 68. As a result of the present redistribution Huron and Perth will have a combined population of 96,572, and will return three members, giving a unit of 32,191 or 72 per cent of the unit of 44,186 for the entire province.
The counties of Bruce and Grey have been mentioned. There again we have reduced the number of ridings from four to three. In the redistribution of 1921 the counties of Bruce and Grey had a combined population of 103,786, and returned four members, giving a unit of 25,946, or 72 per cent of the average of 35,776. Under the present redistribution these two counties will have a combined population of 99,985, and will return three members, giving a unit of 33,328, or 74 per cent of the unite of 44,186 for the entire province.
Under the present redistribution there will only be a few counties left in all Ontario that will have their own boundaries as the boundaries of their new ridings. That gives the house some idea of the changes that have had to be made throughout Canada as a result of the increase in the population of the
province of Quebec, which population, as hon. gentlemen know, is divided by sixty-five, representing its representation in this house, in order to give the unit for all Canada. In my opinion that is one of the saving clauses of the British North America Act. If it were not for that clause this house would likely be twice its present size. I believe this country is over-governed to-day. By that I mean that there are altogether too many members of parliament, senators, legislative councillors and members of legislatures. To put it in another way, too many men are engaged in the government of Canada and its provinces. That saving clause in the British North America Act I hope will never be removed.
The counties of Brant, Durham, Elgin, Glengarry, Haldimand, Essex, Wentworth, Welland, Lincoln, Lanark, Middlesex, Norfolk, Northumberland, Leeds, Prescott, Peel, Halton, Renfrew, York and Waterloo are the only counties in this provinoe to-day that it is not proposed to associate under this redistribution with other counties, and I doubt if in the next redistribution there will be more than two or three counties in that category.
Something has been said about the counties having a smaller population as the result of the present redistribution, but under the present redistribution the following rural communities will have a larger unit than the county of Perth, namely, Nipissing, Welland, Wentworth, East York, West York, South York, Waterloo and Kent.
Reverting to what was said about the cities, the city population has very considerably increased since the last redistribution. Brantford has increased in population by approximately one thousand, but its representation has not been increased. Fort William has increased by approximately six thousand, and the increases in other cities have been as follows:

I want to say that the committee did work hard. They tried to give an opportunity to every member from Ontario, and they tried to maintain the county boundaries wherever possible, but that could not be done in every case. Every member of the committee regretted that in the end we had to do what we finally did in connection wdth Perth, and Huron, but I cannot see that there is anything else to do. If you make the county of Perth a one-member constituency you would then have two adjacent counties, one of which will have a population of 51,392, returning one member, and the other with 45,180, returning two members. That would hardly be fair to either the county of Huron or the county of Perth. So w'e had to put them together. All we could do was to strengthen North Huron in population, and we did that by adding two municipalities to North Huron, bringing its population up to 26,095, and then we took two townships in Perth South adjacent to Huron and added them to Huron-Perth, making the latter's population 22,656. I agree that that is a small population. Under this redistribution there is one riding left in the province of Ontario which will have a population of only 18,000 odd. I am not going into that question now. Under the previous redistribution there were also a number of ridings with a very small population. Generally speaking, the unit in Ontario has been raised. Although I have not the figures before me there are more ridings as proposed in Ontario to-day close to and over the unit than there were as the result of the last redistribution. I am not criticizing those in charge of the previous redistribution. There is no doubt that hon. members at that time met the same difficulties as those with which we are confronted and no doubt they had to do the best they could. We endeavoured to do our best, and could do only what we did. As a result of the last redistribution ten or twelve members had to contest in five or six seats. The committee which acted at this session I believe may look with a feeling of satisfaction upon the fact that of the eighty-two Ontario seats there is only one in which we had to place two men now in the house. If the whole of Perth county had been put together South Huron would have been left wdth a population of less than 20.000, and we would not have been acting fairly to the county of Perth. I cannot help thinking that we have done our best.

None of us claims that the redistribution is perfect. I say to-day as I have stated before that until we have legislation to conform to that of many other countries, and to that of two provinces in Canada, namely Nova Scotia and Ontario, in which legislation has been enacted stating a minimum unit of population per riding, there will always be some anomalies. I believe however that there have been fewer this time than on any previous occasion, and that the redistribution in the province of Ontario wdll result in fewer heartburnings than any previous redistribution has caused.
May I close by stating that the hon. member for South Perth and the hon. member for North Perth have both been very kind in what they have said about the redistribution since they have known what is proposed. Neither has been harsh in his criticism. Both have acted like real men. I am sure, that they realized the committee had a very difficult task, and that it did the best it could.

Mr. Chairman, I
should like to say only a word or two in reply to the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol). He has compared the population in the two Hurons with the population in the two Perths. I do not wish my remarks to be misinterpreted when I pqint out that the proposal is to take the town of Clinton, which has voted Conservative by a good sized majority, and the township of Goderich, which is largely Conservative, and both of which are now in South Huron, and place them in North Huron constituency. Then, after taking out the town of Clinton and the township of Goderich, in order to adjust the population it is proposed to take these two townships from one riding and put them into South Huron. That constituency is Liberal, and has been Liberal for years. In that instance the committee has used a double edged sword. It is endeavouring to build up a stronger riding for the hon. member representing North Huron (Mr. Spotton). But on the other hand by shifting these two townships into South Huron, the committee has endeavoured to weaken the Liberal candidate in the county of Perth.
I shall offer a solution to the hon. member from Toronto. If he accepts my suggestion in the spirit in which I offer it he can leave North Huron as it is. If this suggestion were adopted rather than the proposed scheme the difference in population would be only a few hundred. The hon. member for North Huron has come through two or three elections successfully, and I feel sure he need

Redistribution-Mr. Slrort
not be afraid of the result. Surely he can come back again. Then the committee could leave South Huron just as it is, there would be no fault to find and the question of population would be adjusted. There would be in each riding of North and South Huron a population of almost 23,000, and the two townships would be left in South Perth as they are at the present time. By accepting my suggestion no one would be adversely affected. Justice would be done not only to the hon. member for North Huron but to the hon. member for South Huron and to myself. Neither would there be any injustice done the hon. member for North Perth. My suggestion is very simple, and would not be very difficult to put into operation. It would adjust this whole grievance.
The hon. member for Toronto Northwest has not given and I suggest he cannot give or will not give the real reason why the townships of Hibbert and Fullarton should be moved from South Perth into South Huron. The only reason is that it would give an advantage to hon. members opposite. Give us an even break on this. Treat us fairly, and you can adjust this matter in five minutes in the way I have pointed out.
' Mr. H. B. SHORT (Digby-Annapolis): For several days we have been listening to a discussion among hon. members from Saskatchewan, Quebec and Ontario. I propose now to say a few words about Nova Scotia. As hon. members are aware, on account of the redistribution, Nova Scotia was obliged to lose two members. And to preserve county lines I have been given a constituency with a population of 50,859. Previous to the last census my constituency had a population of 34.650. It is composed of the counties of Digby and Annapolis. When we realized it was necessary to lose two seats in the province of Nova Scotia, one on the island of Cape Breton and the other on the mainland those people familiar with the map of Nova Scotia expected the counties of Colchester and Pictou would have to be joined. Colchester was the smallest county in the province, having a population of only 25,051. We naturally expected, those of us in the western part of the province, that that constituency would be joined with Pictou and Cumberland. There was another way it might have been divided. There is the county of Antigonish-Guys-borough, represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Duff) and having a population of only 25,560. That adjoins the county of Pictou. There was a suggestion put before the committee that the county of Pictou be divided and half joined with Antigonish-Guysborough, which
would bring that constituency up to the unit number, and let the western part of Pictou county take on Colchester. But the committee did not accept this proposal, they preferred to keep the county lines, which I realize ,are very highly regarded in my province. We have not yet, I think, in any redistribution disturbed county lines except in my county of Digby where they have been disturbed in practically every redistribution. We have in the county of Digby two municipalities, Digby and Clare, which latter is composed of Acadian French, having their own municipal council. In 1911 that municipality was joined with Yarmouth. In the redistribution of 1924 Clare was taken away from Yarmouth and rejoined with Digby-Annapolis. I felt and still feel that I am being legislated out of my seat in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis. I feel that there was another way in which the seats in Nova Scotia could have been redistributed. However, I realize that when these redistributions take place someone has to make sacrifices. My turn has come, and I suppose I shall have to make the best of it. However, I do not like it and I protest against it most vigorously. Personally I feel it very keenly, and more keenly on behalf of my constituents and those who come after me, because it is going to make it utterly impossible for a Conservative to win that seat. Whatever my friends from Ontario and Saskatchewan and Quebec may say about everything in this redistribution having been done for the advantage of the Conservative party, I want to say that as far as Nova Scotia is concerned every advantage has been given to our Liberal friends. As I say, they take the municipality of Clare and join it to Yarmouth which has always given a Liberal majority. In the last three elections I am happy to say I reduced the Liberal majority very materially, and we have almost broken even; however it has been traditionally Liberal since confederation. That district is given to my hon. friend the member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), making his majority the greater. I have had attached to my constituency the county of Kings, which has 24,357 population. It has given a Liberal majority since confederation, with just two exceptions. In the last election the hon. member for Ilants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) had a majority in Kings county of over 900. I feel that I would be lax in my duty to my constituents if I did not make a protest in connection with the redistribution in Nova Scotia.
This constituency in length is 145 miles. It is in one of the most thickly populated districts of Nova Scotia, the Annapolis valley.
